passage: I'm Jagdish, and I work two desks from Afreen. I noticed something change this winter. Afreen used to be first to leave on Fridays for the cinema, and now leaves early to sit with Afreen's mother. Once I passed Afreen in the corridor on the phone, saying, "No, Amma, tell me what you'd like for your birthday. I won't decide for you." Another day Afreen was quiet over lunch and looked at the wall for a while, then said only, "She's got so thin." I asked if Afreen was alright and got a small smile. I can't say what Afreen was feeling. But those early Fridays have not stopped, and last week Afreen showed me a photo of a plate of sweets the two of them had made together.

qa.q: Who is Jagdish in relation to Afreen?
qa.a: A colleague who works two desks away.

qa.q: What does Afreen's remark "She's got so thin" and the long look at the wall suggest?
qa.a: That Afreen has noticed the mother growing frail and is feeling something heavy about it, though Jagdish says Jagdish cannot know exactly what.

qa.q: What is Afreen doing that works better than avoiding visits?
qa.a: Afreen leaves early each Friday to spend real time with the mother and asks what she wants, for example for her birthday, instead of deciding for her.

qa.q: How might Afreen's mother experience those Friday visits?
qa.a: Probably as being cherished and heard, since she is asked what she wants and the two make sweets together, as the photo shows.

grounding: Shows seeing a parent grow frail with fear of loss, the protagonist spending real time now and asking about their wishes, seen by an observer who cannot know their inner state.

passage:
Sarika had skipped three Sundays at her mother's flat in Salt Lake. Work, she told herself. The truth was simpler: every visit, Amma looked smaller.

This Sunday she went. Lavanya was at the window, a shawl over her shoulders in April, and when she poured the tea her hand trembled so much the cup rattled on the saucer. Sarika's chest went tight. What if something happened and she didn't know what to do? What if she was not enough?

She took the pot gently. "Let me." Then, instead of checking her phone, she sat on the floor by Amma's chair. "Amma, is there anything you want to do this year? Anything at all?"

Lavanya was quiet, surprised. "I'd like to see the Durga pujo at my old para once more. And I want my books to go to the school library."

Sarika wrote both down. She stayed until dark and came back on Wednesday.

qa.q: How many Sundays had Sarika skipped?
What was Sarika afraid of when she saw her mother's hand tremble?
qa.a: Sarika felt a tight fear of losing her mother and of not being enough if something happened.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that eased the fear into action?
qa.a: She stayed and sat close, asked her mother what she wanted this year, wrote down the answers and came back on Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt when Sarika asked about her wishes?
qa.a: Lavanya was surprised and probably glad to be asked, since she answered with two clear wishes.

grounding: The passage shows someone who fears losing a frail parent and has been avoiding visits, then chooses to spend real time and ask about the parent's wishes.

passage:
"You're here for twenty minutes again?" Pallavi said, arms folded in the hallway. "Aai fell last week, Uday."

"I know. I know." Uday stared at the shoe rack. "Every time I come, she's thinner. I sit there and I don't know what to say. I can't fix any of it."

"Nobody's asking you to fix it."

"I'm scared, Pallu. Of the phone ringing at night. Of being useless when it does."

Pallavi's face softened. "So am I. That's why I need you here, not in the car with the engine running."

From the bedroom, their mother called, "Are you two fighting?"

Uday went in and sat on the bed. "Aai, can I ask you something? After the fall, do you want to stay in this flat, or come to us?"

She looked at him for a long moment. "Nobody asked me that yet. I want to stay. With a bell by the bed."

"Then we'll get a bell," Uday said, and stayed for dinner.

qa.q: What did Aai want after her fall?
qa.a: She wanted to stay in the flat, with a bell by the bed.
Uday was scared of the phone ringing at night and of being useless when it did.

qa.q: Why was asking his mother about her wishes a good step for Uday?
qa.a: It gave him something real to do with his fear, turned a short visit into real time together, and respected her choice.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Uday's short visits?
qa.a: Pallavi feels frustrated and left alone with it at first, then understanding once she hears he is scared too.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young man afraid of losing his frail mother who has been keeping visits short, then staying and asking about her wishes.
